Senses.Explanation: The term names the named teacher in each cited record’s recorded act of approving or certifying a person’s understanding; the entries keep that act distinct from assigning succession. Literally, "seal" (印) and "approve or permit" (可): "approve and certify," attested 761 times in 173 allowlisted texts. Lamp and lineage records use the verb for recorded acts of approval. After a student opens to understanding at Tianyi's assembly, Tianyi "approves him, saying: this is my house's thousand-mile colt" (印可曰，此吾家千里駒也). Another account says an unnamed interlocutor approved six people individually and told them, "you six people together verify my body; each accords with one part" (汝等六人，同證吾身，各契其一). Narrative forms include "all received approval" (皆蒙印可), "deeply received approval" (profoundly receiving the seal of approval), and "received the named record subject's approval" (receiving an unnamed interlocutor’s seal of approval). These passages record approval, the named record subject's words at approval, and who received it; they do not make every occurrence a single theory of what was certified.
Senses.Note: Approval is not always the end of examination. In the Zhang Shangying case, after Donglin has approved the commissioner, Doushuai asks whether he still has any doubt about the words and teachings of buddhas and ancestral teachers. Historical notices also distinguish a person's approving teacher from the lineage teacher ultimately named in succession: one person can receive approval from more than one unnamed interlocutor while a later record names a particular succession relation. The headword records the approval event; lineage assignment remains a separate structural claim.

Senses.Explanation: Chan records load the ordinary printing block into a criticism of sayings and conduct reproduced from fixed models. One record asks, 'what is block-stamped?' and answers: people who grope along walls, have no genuine understanding of their own, and rely entirely on ancient sayings as a staff. Another defines 'printing-block Chan' as reading the records of Yuanwu, Dahui, and Zhongfeng and turning out something resembling them. The widespread paired formula says that teachers or learned sayings are 'stamped from a printing block and released from a mold,' then contrasts this with responding as circumstances arise. The Zen deviation is this printing-shop language for publicly criticized, model-bound Chan speech; the term does not merely mean generic sameness.

Senses.Explanation: "different kinds." In Chan questions it can stand alone: asked "what are the other kinds?" (如何是異類), the identified master strikes a bowl and calls a servant to eat, while another answers "the foot is short, the inch is long" (尺短寸長). Its defining Zen deployment is the fixed expression "move among other kinds" (異類中行). Nanquan says people of the time must move among other kinds; challenged on "kind," he puts both hands on the ground. Another witness places the expression beside "although moving in an animal's conduct, one does not receive an animal's recompense" (雖行畜生行，不得畜生報). Cao Dong's record supplies the sharpest lexical boundary: the ancients provisionally borrowed the water buffalo as an "other kind"; it is an other kind in the matter, not an other kind in language (古人權借水牯牛為異類。秖是事上異類。非言語中異類). The entry records these answers and boundaries without deciding what spiritual condition they express.

The phrase names movement or conduct “among different kinds,” and Chan records make it a contested classification of how a person goes rather than a zoological destination. Nanquan Puyuan says that Chan monks “must move among different kinds” (須向異類中行), answers Guizong Zhichang’s animal-conduct objection, and elsewhere classifies Daowu Yuanzhi’s withdrawal from an exchange as “moving among different kinds” (他却是異類中行). Caoshan Benji repeats Nanquan’s classification while discussing forms of speech. Langting Ting distinguishes moving among different kinds without cutting off sound and form as the “following fall” (隨墮), alongside the kind-fall and honored-fall. Xieyun Ji uses the phrase of a cat in a playful letter, while Juelang Daosheng tells Huang that earlier people required moving among different kinds and contrasts this with being soaked dead in still water. The shared wording therefore covers named conduct, classification, question-and-answer, and later explanation; the records do not reduce these deployments to a single animal act.

Six curated occurrences from five files and four independent works meet the depth floor without counting parallel editions. Nanquan’s two occurrences belong to one work and provide two distinct deployment shapes, not two sources.
